summary.text: A 65-year-old female developed difficulty speaking and hand shaking when fatigued, which the family suspected to be dementia. Over the following months she could not converse, showed abnormal behavior, had incontinence and wandered, and was admitted to psychiatry for about one month after a dementia diagnosis. Symptoms fluctuated with repeated admissions until a sudden disturbance of consciousness led to emergency hospitalization.

Ammonia was 247 μg/dL at admission and liver cirrhosis was not identified. A non-cirrhotic portosystemic shunt with SMV-IVC as the main shunt vessel was present, classified as Type B hepatic encephalopathy. Flapping tremor was present and EEG showed multiple triphasic waves before treatment; coma was graded II to III before treatment.

She received only conservative treatment with intravenous branched-chain amino acids and oral lactulose and no embolization. Triphasic waves disappeared after conservative treatment and coma was graded I to II afterwards. After several years of follow-up her status is unknown.

summary.text: An 82-year-old female with a history of colon cancer surgery, including partial resection of the ascending transverse colon, was admitted to a local hospital with recurrent remission of psychiatric symptoms and disturbance of consciousness. Hyperammonemia was found during hospitalization and she was referred and hospitalized.

Ammonia was 169 μg/dL at admission and liver cirrhosis was not identified. A non-cirrhotic portosystemic shunt with SV-IVC as the main shunt vessel was present, classified as Type B hepatic encephalopathy, with coma graded II to III before treatment.

Conservative treatment was somewhat successful but not sufficient, so B-RTO was performed and symptoms improved, with consciousness clear afterwards. Ammonia improved to about 100 to 130 μg/dL at hospital discharge, and she remained under follow-up.

summary.text: A 73-year-old male started hemodialysis for diabetic nephropathy, with atrial fibrillation and cerebral infarction listed in his past history. He was admitted to nephrology for disturbance of consciousness and diagnosed with hyperammonemia of unknown origin. Dizziness, nausea, restlessness and somnolence persisted after discharge, and he was referred and admitted to the authors' hospital.

Ammonia was 435 μg/dL at admission and liver cirrhosis was not identified. A non-cirrhotic portosystemic shunt with SV-LRV as the main shunt vessel was present, classified as Type B hepatic encephalopathy, with coma graded II to III before treatment.

Conservative treatment was somewhat successful but not sufficient, so B-RTO was performed and symptoms improved, with consciousness clear afterwards. Ammonia improved to about 100 to 130 μg/dL at hospital discharge. After several years of follow-up he passed away.

summary.text: A 74-year-old female started hemodialysis for diabetic nephropathy and subsequently cycled in and out of hospital with transient disturbances of consciousness and shunt problems. Hyperammonemia from a splenorenal shunt was suspected and she was followed with symptomatic treatment. After the end of hemodialysis her level of consciousness decreased with temporary improvement, then conditions worsened, oral intake became impossible and conjugate deviation of the eyes to the left appeared, and she was transferred.

Ammonia was 318 μg/dL at admission and liver cirrhosis was not identified. A non-cirrhotic portosystemic shunt with SV-LRV as the main shunt vessel was present, classified as Type B hepatic encephalopathy, and imaging showed abnormal vessels from the splenic vein to the left renal vein. Coma was graded II before treatment; EEG showed theta waves, the Hasegawa scale was 10 points, Fischer’s ratio 1.21 and the ICG test 41.8% (corrected R15).

Conservative treatment was somewhat successful but not sufficient, so B-RTO was performed and symptoms improved, with consciousness clear afterwards. Theta waves decreased, the Hasegawa score was 27 points, Fischer’s ratio 2.13 and the ICG test 26.8%, and ammonia did not fluctuate after embolization. After several years of follow-up she passed away.

article_limitations: The article is a four-patient series with several cohort-level statements; only statements naming a case or covering all four patients explicitly were assigned to individuals.
Calendar years are masked in the source (19XX, 200X); times are kept as printed relative expressions.

Imaging basis (contrast-enhanced CT and balloon-occluded retrograde venography) and absence of liver biopsy are stated for the series, not per patient, so they are not recorded as individual procedures.
The "all patients" recurrence clause is kept review_only for each patient because the same sentence cannot apply to case 1, which had no embolization.
The cause of death is stated jointly for cases 3 and 4 and is kept only as an ambiguity, not as each patient's documented cause.
Fischer ratio and ICG values for case 4 are stated as "from X to Y" without measurement times; Hasegawa and EEG are stated before and after treatment without dates.
Case 4 plot values (Figure 1) and image-printed text are pixel content for the visual record only, not facts.
The Japanese-language PDF supplement is a translation of the article; all eight pages were reviewed in the supplement manifest and document sidecar as background that adds no separate clinical facts.
Case 1 is described only through its conservative-treatment outcome; the supplement and text both say its later status is unknown.
